chunks: Stepper advantages over other motors. The question: What are its advantages compared to other types of motors?
The main advantage of a stepper is that it gives accurate, repeatable positioning without feedback.
A brushed or brushless (BLDC) motor spins at a speed set by voltage, so you need a sensor and a control loop to stop at the right place. A stepper moves a fixed angle per pulse.
That makes it cheap and easy to use.
Picture a staircase versus a ramp. On a staircase, you can only stand on certain steps, so counting steps tells you your height.
On a ramp, you can stop anywhere, so you need to look and judge where you are. A stepper is the staircase and a DC motor is the ramp.
The analogy has a gap: if you are pushed hard enough, a stepper can skip a step without telling you.
Shapes, not data. A stepper's usable torque collapses with speed because winding inductance slows the current and back-EMF eats the voltage.
A brushed DC motor's torque only falls linearly towards its no-load speed, and a BLDC with field control holds it flat up to base speed.
If your operating point is to the right of about 600 to 1000 rpm, the stepper is usually the wrong motor.
Open loop: control with no position feedback. Holding torque: torque at zero speed that holds the position. Encoder: a sensor that reports the shaft's position.
Missed step: a step the motor fails to make under overload. Control loop: electronics that compare where the motor is with where it should be, and correct it.
A stepper has 200 steps per turn and drives a lead screw (a threaded rod that turns rotation into straight-line motion) that moves 2 mm per turn. Each step moves 2 / 200 = 0.
01 mm. To move a carriage 10 mm, send 10 / 0. 01 = 1,000 pulses . No encoder or tuning is needed, and the carriage holds position when it stops.
That is the whole idea: one pulse is one known movement.

"A stepper's big advantages are open-loop positioning without an encoder or tuning, full holding torque at standstill, high torque at low speed so it can drive loads directly, no brushes, and low cost with a simple step/dir interface; error also doesn't accumulate.
The downsides are torque falling with speed, low efficiency and heat because it always draws full current, resonance, and silent missed steps.
So steppers win on cost and simplicity at low speed, and servos or BLDCs win on speed, efficiency and knowing their position."
